item.title: Nintendo Switch 2's New Game Gifting Feature Comes With One Catch for Your Friends List
item.description:
Nintendo is finally giving Nintendo Switch 2 owners a direct way to buy digital games for other people, and it's a feature I've wanted to see on the Switch eShop for a long time. Announced on November 9, the new gifting option is coming to both Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 during the week of November 16. Players will be able to purchase eligible games, DLC, and upgrade packs for someone else, rather than sending an eShop gift card and leaving that person to complete the purchase. It's a welcome change, especially with the holiday season approaching. There's a catch, though: the recipient has to be in the sender's Nintendo Account family group.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That requirement takes some of the excitement out of the announcement for me. Nintendo already lets players build friends lists, so those contacts seem like the natural people to send games to. I can imagine wanting to surprise a friend with a co-op game so we could play together that evening, or picking up a smaller title I think they'd love. Under Nintendo's new rules, having someone on my Switch 2 friends list won't be enough. The two of us would also need to belong to the same family group, which can hold only eight Nintendo Accounts in total. For a feature built around giving presents, that's an awkward place to draw the line.

Nintendo Making Big Change to Digital Switch Games

Nintendo announces a major change coming to its digital games that will overhaul the way digital games function on the Nintendo Switch.

By Charming Holiday

Nintendo Switch 2's Digital Gifting Makes Sense for Families, but Not Every Friend

To Nintendo's credit, the actual gifting process sounds refreshingly straightforward. On an eligible Nintendo eShop product page, buyers can check a “Give as a Gift” option, choose someone from their family group, and select which of that person's linked consoles should receive it. There's even a choice of gift wrapping before checkout. The present then appears on the recipient's HOME Menu, ready to be accepted and played. Parents buying games for their children stand to benefit immediately, and I like that the recipient gets a specific game instead of a code or store credit. Giving a friend a game should be easier than reorganizing a Nintendo Account family group.

The problem is that a Nintendo family group isn't the same thing as a circle of gaming friends. A group can include ordinary accounts, so Nintendo isn't insisting that everyone be related. But its eight-person limit includes the administrator, and each account can belong to only one group at a time. Someone whose group already includes family members may have no room for the friends they play with most often. Switching groups just to buy a birthday present isn't a great solution, either. Nintendo warns that repeatedly joining and leaving groups can trigger restrictions, while changing groups can affect who receives benefits from a Nintendo Switch Online family membership. That's a lot of account management for something as simple as buying somebody a game.

Giving a friend a game should be easier than reorganizing a Nintendo Account family group.

What makes the restriction especially strange is that Nintendo solved part of this problem nearly 19 years ago. Back in December 2007, the Wii Shop Channel added an option to purchase eligible downloadable games for registered Wii Friends. Players could choose a game, select a friend, and send it as a present. The store even warned customers when their chosen recipient already owned the game, which helped avoid duplicate purchases. That system had limits of its own: both Wii consoles needed the same country setting, and gifting only covered supported software. Still, Nintendo didn't require people to share a family group before one could buy a game for the other.

Other digital storefronts show why Nintendo's approach feels behind the times. Xbox lets customers send eligible games to friends-list contacts or an email address, subject to regional rules. Steam supports gifting between friends and expanded its options in July 2026 to include purchases through shared wishlists and email delivery. Neither service is completely restriction-free, but both offer a much more natural way to send somebody a game. Nintendo has added other limits, too: supervised accounts can't send gifts, some digital products won't qualify, and gift purchases are subject to an unspecified frequency cap. Gifts also arrive immediately rather than on a chosen date.

Nintendo Should Let Players Send Gifts to Their Friends Lists

I can see why Nintendo started with family groups. The company already uses them for supervised accounts and household services, so they're an existing connection between players. It's a useful setup for parents who want to buy a game for their children without handling a gift card. What I want to see is an option for gifting directly to people on a Nintendo friends list, with sensible purchase and regional safeguards. Nintendo could keep family gifting exactly as it is while giving everyone else a much easier way to share games.

Nintendo Switch 2's New Game Gifting Feature Comes With One Catch for Your Friends List
Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake's Datamined Master Quest Files Come With One Catch
Call of Duty: MW4 Has Basically Ruined Its Best Game Mode
Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Already Reaches Big Sales Milestone

There's a real opportunity here for Nintendo to make its digital storefront feel more social. A friend could send someone a game they've been talking about for weeks, or buy an extra copy of a co-op favorite so they can jump in together. I'd love to see that become a normal part of owning a Switch 2. Nintendo deserves credit for finally announcing a direct gifting feature for its current consoles, and I expect plenty of families will enjoy it. But some of the best gaming memories happen with people outside our households. The next step should be letting us buy presents for those people without asking them to join our family groups first.

item.title: Gorgeous New Steam Creature Collector Turns Pokemon Into a Satisfying Roguelite
item.description:
There's no denying that Pokemon is quite literally everywhere, and it has been since shortly after it was first revealed in the VHS advertisements it sent out back in 1995. Since then, the idea of centering a video game around collecting strange creatures has become immensely popular, to the point that Pokemon is far from the only franchise doing it anymore. In fact, if you take a short little jaunt on Steam these days, you're likely to find more creature collectors than you can count—though that's not necessarily a bad thing for players like me who thoroughly enjoy the genre. The trick, though, is finding a good one, which has become increasingly harder with the advent of AI. Even so, my latest journey through Steam's seemingly endless library of indie games had me stumble upon a game called Wilderings: The Lost Spring , which takes Pokemon 's familiar formula and gives it a satisfying roguelike twist.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I recently spent just under an hour with Wilderings: The Lost Spring 's free demo on Steam, and I have to say, this gorgeous little creature collector is already showing a lot of promise ahead of its Early Access release. The game follows a young woman named Abi as she ventures into a world devastated by a mysterious corruption, with the ultimate goal of restoring its once-thriving ecosystems. Along the way, she befriends creatures known as Hantu, which are basically Pokemon that can be used both in combat and exploration. Where Wilderings differs from traditional creature collectors, though, is in its roguelike structure, which sees Abi embarking on repeated expeditions into the corrupted world, battling enemies, collecting upgrades, and gradually restoring the land to bring even more Hantu back. Between runs, she can return to her floating skyship to strengthen her companions, unlock permanent upgrades, and prepare for whatever comes next.

New Open-World Game Is Like Pokemon Meets Stardew Valley, and It Has 10/10 Reviews

A new open-world game on Steam earns rave reviews from players, making it a perfect pick for fans of Pokemon and Stardew Valley.

By Mohsen Baqery

Wilderings Is a Gorgeous, Addictive Take on Pokemon's Established Formula

Check Out Wilderings: The Lost Spring's Free Demo on Steam

Now, whenever someone claims a game is similar to Pokemon , it's easy to assume that it's all about collecting creatures and nothing more. After all, that is precisely the main draw of Pokemon , and it always has been—gotta catch 'em all, am I right? However, Pokemon has nonetheless been about more than merely catching and collecting monsters, and has instead emphasized befriending them and using them in battle, as well as discovering the world itself. Wilderings: The Lost Spring adopts that same philosophy, only this time, its "trainer," if you will, can actually participate in combat and exploring the world is less about discovery and more about restoration and harmony.

Wishlist Today

Scattered throughout Wilderings ' dying world are Springs that need to be restored, or "rewilded." Upon attempting to rewild a Spring, though, enemies called Vlugkin begin attacking Abi, and even before she has the help of some friendly Hantu, she can retaliate with her own set of combat maneuvers. They're fairly simple, mind you, and largely boil down to a light attack, a heavy attack, and a ranged attack, but she can learn more combat skills as she progresses—more on that later. Once a Spring has been restored, the corrupted area around it comes to life with fresh, green vegetation, and it looks incredible, but the primary appeal of restoring a Spring is actually in the potential rewards it offers.

Like any good roguelike, Wilderings rewards players for restoring a Spring by offering them a selection of cards that can either temporarily buff Abi's own combat abilities, grant passive buffs to her stats, or, and this is the best part, give her a new Hantu companion. Of course, only one of these cards can be selected each time, but selecting a Hantu will permanently unlock that Hantu for players to choose as their starting Hantu ahead of their next run. At the start, you can only have one Hantu with you, but there are enough slots that players can actually have four Hantu following them around as they explore the corrupted land of Wilderings .

Like Pokemon, Hantu can assist in combat, whether that be by attacking enemies or supporting Abi with healing on command. Between runs, they can even be upgraded by feeding them the appropriate fruit, and they can be temporarily upgraded mid-run as well, should players get lucky enough to find a card that buffs their Hantu in some way. Furthermore, players can find any Hantu they've collected wandering around their base between runs, giving a more immersive benefit to finding them by making them feel like actual companions rather than glorified weapons stuffed inside a Poke Ball or PC box.

Back at their base, players can also upgrade Abi through a fairly sizable skill tree, as well as Hantu they've collected via their own skill tree. The base itself can also be enhanced by unlocking various upgrades that can improve Abi's subsequent runs, and the upgrades even add a little extra visual flair to the base. There is also an encyclopedia of all the different Vlugkin players have encountered during runs, with information about their strengths and weaknesses, as well as information on the various Hantu they've collected and where they can be found. Based on what I saw during the demo, there are several different biomes in Wilderings ' world, each with their own unique Hantu to find, giving players plenty of potential discoveries ahead of them.

Wilderings Still Needs Some Polish, But I'm Already Looking Forward to More

As much as I enjoyed my time with Wilderings: The Lost Spring , I do think it needs a bit more polish before it's ready for Steam Early Access, particularly when it comes to performance. During my time with the demo, I encountered some pretty noticeable lag that made combat more frustrating than it needed to be, and at one point, the game actually lagged so badly that I ended up dying because I couldn't properly react to what was happening. That's especially unfortunate for a roguelike, where a single mistake can mean losing an entire run, and it certainly made me a little more cautious about how much I was willing to push forward. Still, considering the game hasn't even launched in Early Access yet, I'm willing to give it some grace, and I'm hoping those performance issues will be ironed out as development continues.

Gorgeous New Steam Creature Collector Turns Pokemon Into a Satisfying Roguelite
Father Accused of Leaving 6-Year-Old Daughter Alone in Line to Buy Pokemon Cards
Pokemon Winds and Waves Might Be Replacing Eevee
Pokemon Red & Blue 30th Anniversary Release Officially Confirmed for April 2027

Even with those issues, though, I genuinely had a difficult time putting Wilderings down, and I think that says quite a bit about what it already has going for it. Its gorgeous visuals initially caught my attention, but it was the satisfying gameplay loop of restoring Springs, collecting Hantu, and gradually growing stronger between runs that ultimately kept me playing. I especially love how the Hantu feel like an actual part of the world, rather than just another collection of creatures to throw at enemies, and I'm curious to see just how much variety the full game will offer. There's still some work to be done, no doubt, but Wilderings: The Lost Spring has already given me more than enough reasons to look forward to getting my hands on it again when it launches in Early Access.

Wilderings: The Lost Spring is still without a Steam Early Access release date, but it's free playable demo is available now.

item.title: Bandai Namco Studio is Permanently Shutting Down
item.description:
Bandai Namco Entertainment confirmed its plans to liquidate and dissolve Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal-based subsidiary that developed the action game Unknown 9: Awakening . Bandai Namco stated that the move was made to ensure long-term growth within its business portfolio.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Four years after it was founded, Reflector Entertainment was acquired by Bandai Namco in September 2020. Despite being based in Canada, Reflector became a subsidiary of Bandai Namco Europe. The only game produced by Reflector in its time with Bandai Namco was Unknown 9: Awakening , an action-adventure title released in October 2024 on Steam, PlayStation, and Xbox. The premise of Unknown 9: Awakening saw players assume the role of Haroona, a woman with the power to explore a mysterious dimension called The Fold. In pursuit of knowledge, Haroona must also fight back against a faction bent on controlling history.

Elden Ring: Path of the Elden Lord is Live Now

Elden Ring: Path of the Elden Lord officially brings players back to the Lands Between with a brand-new release.

By Daniel Morris

Bandai Namco is Closing Reflector Entertainment

Although Unknown 9: Awakening showed off some potential in its action-focused gameplay, which was compared to games like Square Enix's Forspoken , Reflector's project received a mixed response on Steam, with only 55% positive reviews. Bandai Namco revealed that it will liquidate and dissolve Reflector Entertainment, as decreed via a resolution passed down by its board of directors. Bandai Namco stated that the decision was made after considering future business plans and how its corporate value could be enhanced in the long run. The company said it would work in compliance with local laws and regulations throughout the process. Reflector released a statement on LinkedIn shortly after Bandai Namco's decision was handed down. The studio stated it would cease all activities effective immediately.

According to Bandai Namco's statement on Reflector, the studio had over 46 million Canadian dollars in share capital and only made CA$14 million in net sales as of March 31, 2026. Although Reflector was also supposed to work on other IPs within Bandai Namco's repertoire in some capacity, the studio's plans never came to pass. Additionally, following the lukewarm response to Unknown 9: Awakening from buyers, Bandai Namco and Reflector subsequently canceled all plans to expand it into a multimedia franchise. At the time, Reflector CEO Herve Hoerdt said that Reflector would see some jobs become redundant due to the financial failure of Unknown 9: Awakening . At the time of Reflector's closure announcement, the Montreal developer's estimated employee count was between 51 and 200.

The studio said it would work with stakeholders and ensure the developers work through the transition. Reflector added that, between future development requirements and the current conditions of the gaming industry, Bandai Namco could not justify further investment in the studio. Given that the gaming industry has been plagued by layoffs throughout the decade, time will tell what the fate of Reflector's current staff will be. Bandai Namco did not offer a timetable for how long the liquidation process would take.

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake's Datamined Master Quest Files Come With One Catch
item.description:
As someone who has been playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time since 1998, I've spent an awful lot of time with its dungeons over the years, to the point that I can still remember solutions to puzzles I haven't encountered in ages. And while I can't state enough how much I've enjoyed the Switch 2 remake, one of its more disappointing aspects is its lack of Master Quest, which has traditionally offered returning players a much more challenging version of the N64 classic. Fortunately, it looks like Nintendo might not be finished with Ocarina of Time just yet, as dataminers have reportedly discovered references to Master Quest buried in the remake's files. However, there's one particular detail about those discoveries that has me wondering whether Nintendo might end up charging players for something that was previously included at no additional cost.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

According to a November 7 report from Nintendo Everything, dataminer MrCheeze discovered several references to Master Quest in the remake's files, including strings labeled "HasMQ," "IsMQModeExist," "NewGameMQ," and "ReleaseMQ." Fellow dataminer OatmealDome subsequently claimed that the mode appears to be associated with DLC ownership, rather than something Nintendo intends to unlock through an ordinary game update. Of course, Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for Ocarina of Time , and there's no guarantee those files will ever amount to anything players can actually download, let alone something they'll be expected to purchase. But if Master Quest does eventually return as paid DLC, I think Nintendo will need to offer considerably more than the same rearranged dungeons we've already experienced in earlier versions of the game.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Amiibo Masks Have One Problem Tears of the Kingdom Avoided

The Ocarina of Time remake's nostalgic amiibo masks won't arrive until 2027, and Tears of the Kingdom shows why that's a missed opportunity.

By Josh Cotts

Ocarina of Time's Master Quest Has Never Required a Separate Purchase

For those unfamiliar with Master Quest, it originally became available to players through a special GameCube bonus disc distributed alongside preorders of The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker in 2003. Rather than introducing a completely different game, Master Quest took the original Ocarina of Time and rearranged its dungeons, introducing different enemy placements and considerably more complicated puzzles while leaving the main story largely unchanged. The mode eventually returned in Ocarina of Time 3D on the Nintendo 3DS, where it could be unlocked simply by completing the main game. That version even mirrored the entire world and made enemies deal twice as much damage, giving returning players another reason to replay the game yet again.

Considering how much Nintendo has done to modernize Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, I actually think Master Quest would be an excellent addition, especially for longtime players who already know where practically everything is located. However, I also have a hard time imagining Nintendo charging extra for what amounts to the same alternative campaign that came included with the 3DS remake more than 15 years ago. The Switch 2 version already costs $59.99, which I don't necessarily consider unreasonable given how much work went into rebuilding the game, but I also don't think players should have to purchase another expansion just to access a mode that was once considered part of the complete experience. And if Nintendo really does intend to sell Master Quest separately, I'd hope the developers have something considerably more ambitious in mind than simply bringing back the old dungeon layouts with updated graphics.

Interestingly, the datamined files don't necessarily suggest Nintendo is planning anything particularly different from the Master Quest players already know. According to Video Games Chronicle's coverage of the discoveries, OatmealDome found evidence of a mirrored world and modified dungeons, including the rather infamous cows appearing inside Jabu-Jabu's Belly. That certainly sounds familiar to anyone who remembers how strange some of the original Master Quest's puzzles could be, although the files are reportedly incomplete, so there's no way to know whether Nintendo has made more substantial changes. And while I wouldn't complain about being able to experience those dungeons with the remake's updated visuals and controls, I'm not convinced that alone would be enough to justify paying for them again.

Rather than introducing a completely different adventure, Master Quest took the original Ocarina of Time and rearranged its dungeons, introducing different enemy placements and considerably more complicated puzzles while leaving the main story largely unchanged.

What's particularly interesting about all of this is that Master Quest's history actually goes back much further than its GameCube release, with the mode originally being developed for the Nintendo 64DD. During a 2015 Iwata Asks interview about Majora's Mask 3D , Eiji Aonuma explained that he had been tasked with rearranging Ocarina of Time 's dungeons, but eventually became more interested in creating entirely new ones instead. That ultimately led to the development of Majora's Mask , which I find especially interesting considering Nintendo is potentially preparing to revisit the very idea that encouraged Aonuma to pursue a different project in the first place. Obviously, I wouldn't expect Master Quest DLC to become an entirely new Zelda game, but I do think there's an opportunity to do more with its original concept than simply reproduce what players received on the GameCube.

A Paid Master Quest Would Need to Give Players More to Discover

Personally, I think the best approach would be for Nintendo to treat a potential Master Quest expansion as an opportunity to create a genuinely different version of Ocarina of Time , rather than simply making the existing adventure more difficult. Rearranging the dungeons would be a good starting point, but I'd love to see the developers introduce completely new puzzles, unexpected enemy encounters, and perhaps even additional secrets that weren't present in any of the previous versions. The remake has already introduced modern movement controls, including manual jumping, and I imagine the developers could come up with some pretty creative challenges by designing puzzles specifically around those improvements. There's also the possibility of expanding the optional content outside the dungeons, especially since the original Master Quest largely left those parts of the game untouched.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Already Reaches Big Sales Milestone
All Great Fairy Fountain Locations in Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake

Of course, none of this will matter if Nintendo eventually decides to release Master Quest as a free update, which I'd be perfectly happy with, especially considering the mode's history. And even the DLC-related references found in the remake's files don't necessarily mean Nintendo intends to charge for it, so there's still a very real possibility that players won't have to spend anything beyond the original purchase price. But if Master Quest does end up being sold separately, I think Nintendo needs to make sure it's worth paying for rather than simply relying on how much people love Ocarina of Time . I've already spent nearly three decades waiting for yet another reason to play this game again, and I'd certainly welcome another one, but I'd much rather pay for an experience that gives me something new to figure out than one that simply has me solving the same rearranged puzzles I already did countless times on my 3DS.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

item.title: The Lord of the Rings' Greatest RPG Idea Is Still Underused in Its Games
item.description:
The Lord of the Rings has had many game adaptations over the years, and while they all take a different approach to the source material, there is a clear divide between the successful and unsuccessful ones. Games like Shadow of Mordor and The Return of the King are standouts, but ill-fated attempts like Gollum are notorious examples of the bad side of Lord of the Rings games. It's been an ongoing journey of hits and misses, and the tides are hopefully turning to bring a new Lord of the Rings game forth that falls in the "hits" camp.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After making great RPGs like Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 and its predecessor, developer Warhorse Studios has been picked as the next team to make a new Lord of the Rings RPG. This is definitely a daunting task for any developer, but Warhorse Studios may be the best possible pick to tackle The Lord of the Rings universe and truly do it justice. Of course, it's too early to know for sure, but the team is well-acquainted with strong RPG mechanics. As the game goes into production, Warhorse Studios hopefully considers focusing on the core Lord of the Rings feature that has been painfully underutilized in its game adaptations: The One Ring.

Elden Ring Is Great, But Kingdom Come 2 Is the Better Open-World RPG

While there are obvious reasons why some might call Elden Ring the greatest modern open-world RPG, it actually pales in comparison to another.

1
By Ollie Tuscarny

The Lord of the Rings' Most Powerful Object Is the Perfect Fit for an RPG Morality System

There are plenty of great games with good morality systems out there, and The Lord of the Rings still has tons of untapped potential in this space. The One Ring is the central focus of the entire franchise, so it's surprising that it hasn't really been utilized that much in game adaptations. Incorporating this Ring into gameplay may have been too challenging or complex for past games to successfully pull off, but Warhorse Studios is hopefully up to the challenge.

Features like the Shadow of Mordor Nemesis System have taken unique approaches to morality and consequences. As great as the Nemesis System is, though, it would be even more fascinating to see how a One Ring mechanic could affect in-game decisions. Warhorse Studios' work on Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 has already demonstrated that the developer is fully capable of crafting complex and reactive consequences when it comes to gameplay. It's what makes Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 such an insanely good RPG. That kind of depth is exactly what is needed to build a strong morality system centered on The One Ring.

Warhorse Studios hopefully considers focusing on the core Lord of the Rings feature that has been painfully underutilized in its game adaptations: The One Ring.

Using The One Ring's Temptation as a Choice-Based Mechanic

  • Players in possession of the Ring have the power to wield it for evil or good.
  • Using the Ring would bring players certain advantages while also adding a countering disadvantage.

It would be entirely up to players if they wished to lead a noble path forward, or take the Ring for one's own power and gain. For example, choosing to wield the Ring could offer enticing special abilities like heightened senses, stronger persuasion, and better health. However, the consequences would be that the surrounding world would plunge deeper into darkness. This would lead to a "bad" ending that sees players ruling over Middle-earth as a tyrant, but there could also be a "good" ending that is more in line with Aragorn's reign in The Return of the King .

Another way that a One Ring morality system could work is by forcing players to give up important items or non-Ring-related perks with every use. This would add some serious stakes to the gameplay instead of making the game a Middle-earth power fantasy. The temptation that The One Ring brings needs to feel just as powerful in-game as Tolkien's writing makes it seem in the books.

Warhorse Studios Has What It Takes to Bring Gamers the Next Great Lord of the Rings Game

As exciting as the new Lord of the Rings game is, it will probably be a while before Warhorse Studios reveals any new information regarding gameplay or story. Really, all that's known right now is that the project is in development, and the developer is building the game with Unreal Engine 5. Switching from the CryEngine to Unreal Engine 5 is a big risk, but Warhorse Studios must have made the decision for a good reason. The studio has also teased a "deeply immersive" RPG experience, which isn't surprising, given how immersive Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is.

New Co-Op Lord of the Rings Game Officially Announced
The Lord of the Rings: Legolas Officially Revealed

With a new Kingdom Come game in the works and this Lord of the Rings project also on the way, Warhorse Studios has its hands full at the moment. Waiting for updates is always frustrating, but it's also important to allow developers the time and space needed to make as strong of a game as possible. There's no way to know what lies in store for players with this new Lord of the Rings game, but it's probably one of my most-anticipated projects at the moment. Tolkien's world is a great base to build fascinating fantasy RPGs from, and the game will be even better if it fully embraces the power of The One Ring.
